public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 387

*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/387](https://www.erdosproblems.com/387)
 - [ErGr76b] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L., *On the prime factors of
   ${n \choose k}$*. Fibonacci Quart. (1976), 348-352.
 - [Er78g] Erdős, Pál, *On prime factors of binomial coefficients. II*. Mat. Lapok
   (1978/82), 307-316.
 - [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial
   number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
 - [Sc58] Schinzel, A., *Sur un problème de P. Erdős*. Colloq. Math. (1958), 198-204.
 - [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
 - [Fa66] Faulkner, M. "On a theorem of Sylvester and Schur." Journal of the London Mathematical
    Society 1.1 (1966): 107-110.
 - [BNPZ26] Bui, H., Naprienko, S., Pratt, K., and Zaharescu, A. Binomial coefficients with
    divisors avoiding an interval. arXiv:2605.21221 (2026).
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter

namespace Erdos387

/--
Is there an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that, for all $1 \leq k < n$, the binomial coefficient
$\binom{n}{k}$ has a divisor in $(cn, n]$?

Bui, Naprienko, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BNPZ26] answered this negatively.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_387 : answer(False) ↔ ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ n k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k → k < n →
    ∃ d : ℕ, (d : ℝ) ∈ Set.Ioc (c * n) n ∧ d ∣ n.choose k := by
  sorry

@[category research solved, AMS 11]
example : ∀ i < 15, ¬ 99215 - i ∣ Nat.choose 99215 15 :=
  fun i hi => by interval_cases i <;> native_decide

/-- The following is Schinzel's conjecture, which appears in [Gu04]. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_387.variants.schinzel : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ᶠ k in atTop, ¬ IsPrimePow k → ∃ n : ℕ, ∀ i < k, ¬ n - i ∣ n.choose k := by
  sorry

/-- It is easy to see that `n.choose k` has a divisor in `[n / k, n]`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_387.variants.easy {n : ℕ} {k : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) (hk : k ≤ n) : ∃ d : ℕ,
    (d : ℝ) ∈ Set.Icc (n / k : ℝ) n ∧ d ∣ n.choose k := by
  by_cases k = 0 <;> simp_all
  refine ⟨(n.choose k).gcd n, ⟨?_, ?_⟩, gcd_dvd_left _ _⟩
  · rw [div_le_iff₀ (by positivity)]
    norm_cast
    rw [← Nat.gcd_mul_right]
    refine Nat.le_of_dvd ?_ (Nat.dvd_gcd ⟨(n - 1).choose (k - 1), ?_⟩ (dvd_mul_right _ _))
    · exact Nat.gcd_pos_of_pos_right _ (by positivity)
    · cases n <;> cases k <;> simp_all [Nat.add_one_mul_choose_eq]
  · exact Nat.le_of_dvd (by linarith) (gcd_dvd_right _ _)

/--
Is it true for any $c < 1$ and all $n$ sufficiently large, for all $1 \leq k < n$,
$\binom{n}{k}$ has a divisor in $(cn, n]$?

This variant appears in [Gu04]. Bui, Naprienko, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BNPZ26] answered it
negatively.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_387.variants.guy : answer(False) ↔ ∀ c : ℝ, c < 1 → ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k →
    k < n → ∃ d : ℕ, (d : ℝ) ∈ Set.Ioc (c * n) n ∧ d ∣ n.choose k := by
  sorry

end Erdos387

findings.description: The Lean statement is `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᶠ k in atTop, ¬ IsPrimePow k → ∃ n : ℕ, ∀ i < k, ¬ n - i ∣ n.choose k`. Its docstring calls this "Schinzel's conjecture". But Schinzel's conjecture, as Erdős recorded it, has an explicit threshold: for EVERY k ≥ 34 (k > 33) that is not a prime power there is an n with no n−i (0 ≤ i < k) dividing C(n,k). `∀ᶠ k in atTop` gives a strictly weaker claim. Schinzel's form implies the Lean form (take K = 34), but not the other way round. The Lean form would still hold if finitely many non-prime-power k ≥ 34 had no such n; Schinzel's conjecture would then be false. A proof of the Lean statement would therefore not prove Schinzel's conjecture. Mitigating point: the Lean copies erdosproblems.com/387 word for word ("for all sufficiently large k which are not prime powers"), and that wording has been stable in the page history since 2025-10-20. That is why this is marked questionable, not misformalization. Everything else in the statement matches the source; see the reformulation entry.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős, On prime factors of binomial coefficients II, Mat. Lapok 30 (1978/82), p. 315 ([Er78g], cited in this file), https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1982-14.pdf. The OCR text reads "most Schinzel sejti, hogy a sejtés hamis minden [k≥]34-re, mely nem p^α alakú, könnyű belátni, hogy ha k=p^α, akkor a sejtés igaz". My translation: "now Schinzel conjectures that the conjecture is false for every k ≥ 34 not of the form p^α; it is easy to see that if k = p^α the conjecture is true." Erdős, Problems and results on consecutive integers and prime factors of binomial coefficients, Rocky Mountain J. Math. 15 (1985), p. 358 (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1985-27.pdf): "About 25 years ago I conjectured that for every k and n such that 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2, (n−i) | C(n,k) for some 0 ≤ i < k. Schinzel found a counter-example ... and Schinzel conjectured that it fails for every k > 33, k ≠ p^α." By contrast, erdosproblems.com/387 (Wayback snapshot 2026-08-24) paraphrases this as "for all sufficiently large k which are not prime powers". I could not read Guy B34, so I do not know which form [Gu04] uses.
findings.suggested_fix: Either state Schinzel's conjecture exactly: `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ k ≥ 34, ¬ IsPrimePow k → ∃ n : ℕ, ∀ i < k, ¬ n - i ∣ n.choose k`. Or keep the `∀ᶠ` form as an explicitly weaker variant and say in the docstring that Schinzel's original threshold is k > 33 ([Er78g, p. 315]). In both cases, write the conjecture out in the docstring.

reformulations.difference: The inner existential `∃ n : ℕ, ∀ i < k, ¬ n - i ∣ n.choose k` uses truncated ℕ subtraction and puts no lower bound on n. The source says "there exists an n such that C(n,k) is not divisible by any integer in (n−k, n]". Erdős's original setting also assumes n ≥ 2k.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Take k ≥ 1. A witness n ≤ k never works: if n < k then C(n,k) = 0, which every number divides; if n = k then i = k−1 gives n−i = 1, which divides 1. For n > k, the numbers n−i with i < k are exactly the integers in (n−k, n], and truncation never happens. I proved in Lean that the Lean form is equivalent to `∃ n, k < n ∧ ∀ d, n - k < d → d ≤ n → ¬ d ∣ n.choose k`. Two further facts, not proved in Lean. (1) No n with k < n ≤ 2k works: by Sylvester–Schur (and Bertrand when n = 2k), some prime p in (n−k, n] divides C(n, n−k) = C(n,k). So the Lean form is also equivalent to requiring n ≥ 2k. (2) "There exists n" is equivalent to "there are infinitely many n". The property is unchanged under n ↦ n + tQ with Q = ∏_{q≤k} q^{e_q} and q^{e_q} > n, because the valuations v_q(n−i) and, by Kummer, v_q(C(n,k)) for q ≤ k do not change. I checked this numerically for k = 15, n = 99215, t = 0..3.

could_not_verify: Erdos387.erdos_387.variants.guy: I could not get the text of Guy's book [Gu04], B33/B34: archive.org blocks search inside the book, and the Springer and Google Books pages are gated. The Lean (∀ c < 1, eventually in n, for all 1 ≤ k < n) matches erdosproblems.com's paraphrase: "Erdős conjectured this is true for any c<1 (if n is sufficiently large)". answer(False) is correct under either quantifier reading, with n₀ depending on c alone or on c and k. BNPZ26 gives infinitely many n, with k fixed in a dyadic range (and, by their covering theorem, a single fixed k), such that C(n,k) has no divisor in (n/B, n].

Erdos387.erdos_387.variants.schinzel: I could not read Guy's B34 wording or Schinzel's 1958 paper (image-only scan). So I cannot tell whether [Gu04] gives the threshold k > 33 (as Erdős does in [Er78g] and in his 1985 paper) or 'sufficiently large' (as erdosproblems.com does). This decides whether the questionable finding above matters relative to [Gu04].
review.notes:
Source access. The live erdosproblems.com and OEIS sites return Cloudflare challenges, so I used Wayback snapshots of erdosproblems.com/387, its LaTeX, its forum thread and its edit history. The page was last edited 2 July 2026; status: SOLVED.

Main theorem `erdos_387` (answer(False)). It matches the source's question word for word, and Erdős–Graham 1976, p. 351 ("Perhaps it is true however, that d_k(n) > cn for a suitable constant c"). The answer is right: BNPZ26 v2 (unconditional) Theorem 1.3 and its corollary give infinitely many C(n,k), with k ≍ (log log n)^{1/2}, that have no divisor in (n·(log log log log n / log log log n), n]. That refutes every constant c > 0. The paper states that the answer to its Question 1.1 (identical to the source's question) is "no".

Guy variant (answer(False)). Also consistent with BNPZ26. Including c ≤ 0 is harmless, since those cases hold trivially with d = 1.

`example`. It correctly checks the Schinzel–Erdős counterexample: the values 99215 − i for i < 15 are exactly the integers in (n−15, n] = [99201, 99215].

`erdos_387.variants.easy`. It is fully proved: `#print axioms` shows only the standard axioms. The k = 0 case uses the junk value n/0 = 0, which is harmless.

Schinzel variant status. `research open` agrees with the sources. BNPZ26's covering proposition gives ≥ K^{1−o(1)} values k ~ K that admit a cover, not all non-prime-power k, and nothing records a resolution.

`answer(sorry)` display. At Prop it elaborates to `True` under the repository's default `google.answer` setting. That is expected and not a defect.

Style only, not a finding. The Schinzel variant's docstring never states the conjecture.
